Most reviews inspect the easy part: seeded data, wide viewport, the request that succeeds. That's what the change does on its best day. The most important thing a review can do is ask what's on screen when the data is empty, when the request fails, when someone arrives by keyboard at 320px.

Catching bugs isn't the most important thing — your tests should do that, and they run on every commit.

The most important thing is whether the next person who reads this code, six months from now, will understand what it does and why. That person is often you.

Code review is one of the few moments two engineers sit with the same code at the same time, and the value lives in what gets transferred between you — intent, the decision you almost made and didn't, the assumption the author stopped noticing three hours in.

If the reviewer leaves without learning anything, and the author leaves without seeing the code through someone else's eyes, the review failed, even if nothing was missed.
